replying_to: Replying to Informative Robust Causal Representation for Generalizable Deep Learning
display_title: Official Review of Paper2366 by Reviewer 3Akd

content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors tackle learning causal representations for robust/generalizable deep learning. Using an assumed causal DAG, and the data processing inequality, they arrive at an objective to optimize that relies on information theoretic quantities. The tractable version of this objective is similar to that of information bottleneck models. Such an objective leads to a learned representation that might conflate causes (i.e., parents) of Y with non-descendant variables of Y. To address this issue, the authors design a minimax approach that also ensures that the learned representation (likely) satisfies the probability of necessary and sufficient cause of Y.
content.main_review:
Strengths: 
- The authors tackle an important topic that is currently receiving a lot of attention in the ML literature. Learning causal/robust representations would be of interest to a wide audience.  
- The authors provide rigorous finite sample analysis of their approach 
- The authors present compelling empirical results that show that their approach outperforms baselines. 

Weaknesses: 

1 - The clarity of the paper is lacking at best. Logical jumps made it a really slow read. Consistent typos make it hard to understand what the authors intend to say. Below is a list of all the typos I was able to catch. This is the biggest weakness of the paper, but it does not factor that much into my score. I trust that if the paper is accepted for publication, the authors would make a non-hasty pass through the writing. 

2- Other issues relating to clarity: 

2a - After theorem 1, the authors say "when the underlying causal information is unavailable from observational data we use eq5 to identify causal information". Can the authors clarify what they mean by that? By causal information, do you mean causal structure? And how do they use equation 5 to identify the causal structure?

2b - what does the dashed line in figure 1(b) between ndy and dcy mean?

3 - None of the results (tables 1, 2 and figure 2) report standard deviations/standard errors, which makes it really difficult to assess if CaRR outperforms the baselines. Would the authors be able to provide these? 

4- Can the authors explain how they arrived at a value of 0.8/-0.8 for b in their experiments section?

5- Can the authors explain why their model seems to give better accuracy under high adversarial attacks as measured by the inf norm? It seems counterintuitive or odd.

Addressing comments 2-5 would improve my score. 

---------- 
Editorial comments/typos:

- 2nd paragraph in introduction, fourth line: taking use --> making use of
- Preliminaries, counterfactual estimation: we should inference the posterior --> we should infer the posterior
- method, section 4.1 fourth line: ascendent nodes --> parent nodes
- method, section 4.1, 4 lines under equation 5: let Z = \phi(X) denotes --> let Z = \phi(X) denote
- method, section 4.1, the line directly below equation 8: the different is --> the difference is
- method, section 4.1 third line below equation 8: indtead --> instead
- method, section 4.2, 2nd and 6th line, and in definition 4: necessity and sufficient --> necessary and sufficient
- method, section 4.2 3rd line from the top of the page: if intervene representation z--> if we intervene on the representation z
- experiments, implementation of our method: the first positive part eq 13 (1) is evaluate --> the first positive part eq 13 (1) is evaluated
- experiments, implementation of our method: while b is a hyperparameter --> where b is a hyperparameter
- experiments, metrics: calsulat --> ? I am not sure what this word is.
- Experiments, result analysis: Alghough --> although
content.summary_of_the_review: The authors present an interesting method to learn the (causal) parents of a variable Y. Issues relating to clarity (point 2 in weaknesses), as well as some of the empirical results/choices (points 3-5 in weaknesses) make me vote for a borderline rejection. If the authors address these weaknesses, I am happy to adjust my score.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 3Akd
content.comment:
We appreciate reviewers’ approval and constructive comments. Incorporating them will surely make the paper into a better shape.

**Q1: The clarity of the paper**:

Thank you for your advise, we have modified typos and improper description in our paper. We will add more description and improve the writing quality consistently. 

**Q2.a: After theorem 1, the authors say "when the underlying causal information is unavailable from observational data we use eq5 to identify causal information". Can the authors clarify what they mean by that? By causal information, do you mean causal structure? And how do they use equation 5 to identify the causal structure?**: 

The sentence means that we only have some observations which are mixed by paY, ndY and dcY and each of them is unknown. We use the minmax approach from Theorem 1 to identify the cause information paY. Theorem 1 also the approach to satisfy inequality in Eq. 5.

**Q2.b: 2b - what does the dashed line in figure 1(b) between ndy and dcy mean?**

The dashed line means that the path between dcY and ndY is bidirectional (either direction is OK).

**Q3: None of the results (tables 1, 2 and figure 2) report standard deviations/standard errors, which makes it really difficult to assess if CaRR outperforms the baselines. Would the authors be able to provide these?**

Thank you for your comment. We do additional 4 experiments for each experimental setting and calculate the average of evaluation metrics and standard error of them, and report them in the last page of Appendix (Table 3-7). It includes Yahoo, PCIC, Coat.

**Q4: Can the authors explain how they arrived at a value of 0.8/-0.8 for b in their experiments section?**

b is a hyper-parameter, and we find that 0.8 will make our method perform well in experiments.  In all baselines, we use the same b.

**Q5: Can the authors explain why their model seems to give better accuracy under high adversarial attacks as measured by the inf norm? It seems counterintuitive or odd.**

It is because we report the results (including AUC, ACC, adv AUC and adv ACC) inferenced by models with best adv AUC in validation dataset. In that case (choose the model with best adv AUC), models of robust mode some times will have better AUC and ACC than models of standard mode. In Appendix, we report additional results inference from models with best AUC in validation dataset, we find that standard mode have better average AUC than robust mode in most cases.

We think that the phenomenon is an evidence that the optimization of CV term helps us to identify the exogenous variables which can help the model find better representations. It shows that our method will enhance the adversarial performance without damaging standard performance a lot.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper tackles the problem of representation learning using only causal covariates for more robust performance. More specific, it designs a new loss function that is the lower bound for the Lagrangian form of a certain optimization problem whose solution is the causal covariates. Finite sample analysis characterizing the gain of using causal covariates for prediction rather than the whole set of covariates is provided,  offering theoretical justification for the good performance of the proposed method. Further, promising empirical results are shown.
content.main_review:
Strengths: 
1. I think this paper tackles an interesting and important question, and providing a practical and sound solution. 
2. The empirical and theoretical justification seems convincing to me.

Weaknesses:
From my side, the biggest weakness lies in the quality of writing. It seems the paper is written in a hectic and there are many typos. And the maths part is a bit sloppy, some of them affects me understanding the method. For example, in definition 3, what does x \in X mean? In Equation (6): Z is used as a dummy variable in first line, yet it seems to have a concrete definition Z=phi(X) according to the first line in Theorem 1 and the second line in Eq(6). It makes me confused. In Eq(13), seems we have Z, Z', \bar Z', but the information in subscript of min seems incorrect. My suggestion is to carefully read through the paper, especially the math part and avoid any typos/vagueness. Besides, I think it would be useful to discuss a bit how the final loss function is used (e.g., what network structure is used? How the minimax loss is approximated/optimized?). Further, in derivation for the final loss, there are many intermediate inequalities. It would be curious for readers to know how tight each bound is: for example, the authors may consider adding discussions on when the equality is achieved, etc..
content.summary_of_the_review: I think this paper has its merits of tackling an important question and providing a practical solution. Yet I believe it is not fully ready for publication at ICLR for now mainly due to the writing quality.

replying_to: Replying to Informative Robust Causal Representation for Generalizable Deep Learning
display_title: Official Review of Paper2366 by Reviewer VnTh

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a novel quantification of the causal effect of the representation on the downstream task and learns robust causal representation from data from the perspective of mutual information. Besides, they depict a quantitative link between the amount of causal information and the sample complexity on downstream tasks. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that the models trained on causal representations learned is robust under adversarial attacks and distribution shift.
content.main_review:
Reasons to accept:
1.	The paper proposes a new way of learning robust representation from observational data, that identifies the parents' node pa_Y under the assumption that the observed variables consist of four latent representations, i.e., X = \{pa_Y,dc_Y,nd_Y,nc\}.

2.	Lemma 1 and the objective function (Eq. 8) coincide with deep Information Bottleneck (IB). The author generalizes the IB setting into causal space. 

3.	The paper proposes a Counterfactual Vulnerability (CV) term to identify a mapping function that learns the representation most likely to satisfy the PNS condition. It reduces the search space of the model and makes it more likely to converge to the optimal solution. 


Reasons to reject: 
1.	Typos in Fig. 1: Decsendants → Descendants; Unify the symbols, pa_y,dc_y,nd_y → pa_Y,dc_Y,nd_Y. 

2.	Important details are missing or confusing, which hurts readability. What pa_Y,dc_Y,nd_Y refer to in the real-world scenarios, and what kind of scene will have such data? 

3.	The paper focuses on learning a mapping function that maps \phi the X to be pa_Y, i.e., \phi(X)=pa_Y and defines pa_Y as the minimal sufficient statistics of Y. One confusing aspect is that dc_Y are colliders in the causal effect estimation of \phi(X)=pa_Y on Y, but the author has been trying to convince readers: pa_Y are confounders and confound the causal relationship between Y and dc_Y. This is true, but it seems even more disturbing for the article. 

4.	Although dc_Y and pa_Y are both closely related to Y, the information Bottleneck theory is sufficient to identify the representation of \phi(X)=pa_Y. The baselines are all before 2017. Comparative experiments with some more compact mutual information estimators and recent IB baselines may be necessary [Belghazi 2018] [Cheng 2020]. 

[Belghazi 2018] Belghazi, M. I., Baratin, A., Rajeshwar, S., Ozair, S., Bengio, Y., Hjelm, D., and Courville, A. Mutual information neural estimation. In ICML, 2018.

[Cheng 2020] Cheng P, Hao W, Dai S, et al. Club: A contrastive log-ratio upper bound of mutual information[C]//International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2020: 1779-1788.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes a new way of learning robust representation from observational data, but some baselines are missing.

content.title: Response to Reviewer VnTh
content.comment:
We appreciate reviewers’ constructive comments. Incorporating them will surely make the paper into a better shape.

**Typos in Fig. 1: Decsendants → Descendants; Unify the symbols,pay,dcy,ndy → paY,dcY,ndY.**:

Great thanks for your advice, we fix the typos in our paper. 

**Important details are missing or confusing, which hurts readability. What paY,dcY,ndY refer to in the real-world scenarios, and what kind of scene will have such data?**

To make it easy to understand, we give an example here. Considering the image classification task on human face, a simple causal mechanism behind the observation is (Gender, Age) -> Smiling -> Narrow eyes, (Gender, Age) -> Smiling -> Beard. In this case, if we want to predict Smiling, (Gender, Age) is paY, Smiling is Y, Narrow eyes is dcY. 

**Colliders and confounders**:

We will enhance our logic to make our paper more understandable. In our paper, paY is the most important variable. The causal effect between paY and Y will decide the mutual information between paY and Y (I(paY;Y)). If there exist any  back-door and front-door path between paY and Y, the causal effect can not be identified. In our confounded case, we considering a situation that if there are confounders between paY and Y, the confounder will be actually absorbed in to paY. paY is actually the confounder between Y and dcY, but we do not focus on I(Y;dcY), in our paper, we mainly focus on I(paY;Y). dcY is the collider, it means the path from paY and Y to dcY is not back-door and front-door path so the mutual information I(paY; Y) will not be influenced by the information of dcY. 

**Baselines on mutual information estimator**:

The proposed method is not a mutual information estimator, we use the [1] to evaluate the mutual information term in our method.  The mentioned two methods [Belghazi 2018] [Cheng 2020] are related to [1] since they are both mutual information estimator and they are both references we added in our related work section.

**References**:

[1] Alexander A Alemi, Ian Fischer, Joshua V Dillon, and Kevin Murphy. Deep variational informationbottleneck.arXiv preprint arXiv:1612.00410, 2016

replying_to: Replying to Informative Robust Causal Representation for Generalizable Deep Learning
display_title: Official Review of Paper2366 by Reviewer vUUL

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a representation learning framework by constructing a hypothetical causal graph corresponding to the (latent) components of data $\mathbf{X}$ and the prediction variable $\mathbf{Y}$. The main aim is to learn a representation such that this representation isolates the causal parents of $\mathbf{Y}$ as per the proposed graph. An information theoretic minimax approach is taken to learn this representation and finite sample complexity bound of generalization ability is obtained.
content.main_review:
The approach assumes two different hypothetical causal graphs, one with confounders and the other without. It should be discussed if its reasonable to expect that the data $\mathbf{X}$ contains all the confounders, and there are no unmeasured confounders. If there are unmeasured confounders (which most likely to be without further knowledge of the data), then the provided analysis is not really applicable. At the very least, it should be mentioned that the analysis assumes causal sufficiency. It also needs to be mentioned if the considered datasets are causally sufficient.

When confounder case is considered, the authors employ a form of mutual information decomposition in Eq. 5. How is the inequality obtained? A short explanation makes it easier to read.

One of the main concerns I have with the presented approach is that its not clear if the causal parents of the variable $\mathbf{Y}$ is identifiable from observational data alone. There is no reference to this result nor theoretical result which discusses it. I am not really sure if the obtained representations are anywhere close to the true causal parents. For example, do you see the generalisation bound close to the ideal case (Eq. 15)? There are no experiments on simple synthetic dataset to verify this. In this regard, most of the analysis is only valid if the causal parents are identifiable.

There are many clarifications and typos which need to be fixed. 
Here are some of them:

  -  What is $\beta$ is Eq. 15?  

  -  In Eq. 7. Isn’t $H(pa_{Y})$ a Lagrangian term with a different Lagrangian parameter? In that case, in the next equation where inequality is obtained, the entropy term does not necessarily cancel out. 

  -  In proof of Lemma 1.2, what is Eq. (23)? Why is $I(\mathbf{X},Y)$ mentioned? In Eq. (22), are $\mathbf{pa_y}$ and $\mathbf{pa_y^{*}}$ different?Also Eq. (20) seems to concern with limit of the Kolmogorov Complexity but Eq. (23) invokes it with mutual information. 

  -  In addition, for Lemma 4, does $H(\mathbf{X})$ corresponds to Shannon entropy but in the analysis with representation learning, are the authors still dealing with Shannon entropy or differential entropy? In the case of latter, are the results still valid?

  - In equation 9, what does $\mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{Z}=\mathbf{z})= y$ refer to? Until that equation, the text assumes $\mathbf{Y}$ as a random variable.

  -  It seems that the final proposed algorithm (or objective function which is computable) is only different from r-CVAE upto a single term. The empirical results seems to be similar too. In this light, r-CVAE needs to be discussed in greater detail (its a non-causal approach) and analyse why a causal view gives rise to this term and how does it influence the results. 

  -  Many of the inequalities obtained should be explained briefly and currently the explanations are missing.

  -  There are many typos throughout the paper.

The authors consider confounded version of the hypothetical graph. But backdoor criterion is not used anywhere to adjust for these confounder variable in their theoretical analysis. In addition, it would be nice to clarify if the causal version of mutual information as given in (Nihat and Polani, 2008) is more suitable for the entire presented analysis instead of just mutual information. Note that confounders can be handled within the definition of (Nihat and Polani, 2008) assuming causal sufficiency and backdoor adjustment formula.

The exposition of the entire algorithm was a bit convoluted. A lot of machinery was introduced and explained just to arrive at equation (5) which is basically the Information bottleneck (IB). While it is interesting on its own that it gives an alternate derivation of IB apart from Rate Distortion theory, it does not require any causal formalism. One could assume it to be just a Bayesian network and still arrive at the same result. 

The proposed algorithm is hence only to disentangle parents of $\mathbf{Y}$ and descendants of $\mathbf{Y}$. PNS is introduced and approximated. But some terms (like $I(\mathbf{Z},Y)$) are dropped to make the objective simpler? How does dropping it affect the proposed final algorithm?

References:

Ay, Nihat, and Daniel Polani. "Information flows in causal networks." Advances in complex systems, 2008.
content.summary_of_the_review: While the proposed approach presents a lot of analysis on using Mutual information and hypothetical causal graph to propose a representation learning approach, the entire exposition is a bit convoluted and ridden with typos and major concerns (see above). In addition, it is not clear if the proposed contribution of finding causal parents is actually achieved. In this regard, I feel the paper is not ready for publication yet.

content.title: Response to Reviewer vUUL
content.comment:
Great thanks for reviewers' comments, which inspires us a lot. We make some explanations and modify improper descriptions based on your suggestions.

**Confounders in hypothetical causal graphs**: Fig.1 left  describes an example causal graph in real world system, which does not require all the variable to be observed.  Fig.1 also does not require that all sufficient paY, ndY and dcY being observed. If there are unmeasured nodes in Fig.1, Eq. 4-7  Theorem 1 and Lemma 1.2 actually hold for both two assumptions as well. It is because that the belief graph will not change if some of the nodes are unobservable. For the limitation of Lemma 1.1, PNS technical is used to make up for a lack of ability and help identifying paY.

**About Eq. 5 and identifiability of paY**: We modify Eq. 5 in our paper. Eq. 5 is obtained by conditional decomposition of mutual information. To make it easy to understand, we add some description for Eq. 5 in new version. 

The identifiability of cause information is guaranteed by the Theorem 1, and the bi-level min-max approach can help us  identify paY. Following Pearl’s three steps of counterfactual learning, PNS (definition 1) and CV term also help us to identify paY. We will add synthetic experiments and more analysis on other real-world data in next version. 

>**What is β is Eq. 15?**:β is defined under Eq. 3 "where ${\epsilon_1}$, ... are assumed to be Gaussian noise’ with a distribution $\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0, \beta\mathbf{I}})$ "

>**Why cancel out H(paY)**:H(paY) actually make bound in Eq. 5 loose, but it could be cancelled out since it is not necessary for finding paY. It is because H(paY) not influence Theorem 1. We change Eq. 7 in paper, that the objective now is directly deduced from Theorem 1 rather than Eq. 5. We also give a more tight bound in Eq. 5 that the new inequality is the same with Eq. 4.

>**Why introduce Kolmogorov Complexity in proof of Lemma 1.2**:The Komolgorov Complexity is a technical trick to deduce the second line in Eq. 22. Eq. 23 may confuse readers, it is a Equation explains how to change the algorithmic mutual information to mutual information. We modify Eq. 23 in Appendix to make it easier to understand. 

>**Concerns of Lemma 4**:Lemma 4 is a background knowledge, and it can help to deduce Eq. 23. When sample size is sufficiently enough, the mean of algorithmic mutual information between any random variable X, Y is equal to their mutual information. The solution can be found in [1]  

>**In equation 9, what does counterfactual distribution refer to?**:$P(Y(Z=z)=y|Z≠z, Y≠y)$ is counterfactual distribution, which means based on the observation that $Z≠z, Y≠y$, the probability of $Y=y$ if $Z$ is intervened to be $z$.

>**r-CVAE needs to be discussed in greater detail**:Note that r-CVAE is not a previous method. It is just the modified version of our method CaRR, which cancel out the negative term of the loss. r-CVAE  only optimizes the positive term in Eq. 13, which aims at finding sufficient cause information. CaRR optimizes both positive and negative terms, which can find sufficient and necessary parents from observational data. It is similar with CVAE in the way of conditional prior in Eq.16. Other implications are totally different.

>**Typos in paper and many of the inequalities obtained should be explained briefly**:We added more explanation of equations and modify some typos in our method. We will improve the writing quality consistently.

**Why not use backdoor criterion**: In our paper, we want to provide a new perspective of understanding causality on information-theoretic level and we use mutual information and some entropy to reformulate the causal graph. No confounder between paY and Y is because if there exist, it will be absorbed in paY. It is known that both the backdoor and front door criterion is the tool to identify the causal effect if there exist confounders. Theorem 1 also helps up to achieve identifiability. Backdoor and front door techniches are not necessary in our framework.

**The exposition ... Bayesian network and still arrive at the same result.**We will enhance our writing to make it easy to be understand. We add more explanations in Eq. 5. As for Bayesian network, the analyzing process actually can be utilized into any belief networks. But the results (e.g. Theorem 1,  Eq. 5 Eq. 12 etc…) in our paper only hold in the causal belief net demonstrated in Figure 1,  which reflects the natural generating mechanism. 

**Why drop out I(Y, Z)**:The first term in Definition 5  min I(Y; Z’)  could be regarded as the process to find the worst Z’ around Z, the process of maximizing the I(Y; Z’) by adjusting parameter $\phi$ ( in Eq. 13 ) could be regarded as optimizing the worst case around Z, if the worst case is satisfied, Z is satisfied. That is why I(Y, Z) can be dropped out.

**References**:

[1]Thomas M Cover. Elements of information theory. John Wiley & Sons, 1999

[2]Judea Pearl. Causality. Cambridge university press, 2009.

content.title: Discussion on identifiability, clarity etc.
content.comment:
Thank you for providing a detailed response to my clarifications. I have to admit I am still not convinced by some of the existing claims regarding identifiability. Theorem 1 only states that if there exists a representation $\mathbf{Z}=\phi(\mathbf{X})$ which is the global minimiser of $I(\mathbf{Z};\mathbf{nd_Y}, \mathbf{dc_Y})$ , then it forms the minimal sufficient statistics of $\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{nd_Y}$. It does not tell whether such a representation which is a global minimiser is possible in the first place. This issue is exacerbated by the assumption that *observed data* $\mathbf{X}$ contains all the parents, descendants and non-descendants of $\mathbf{Y}$ (Lemma 1). I am not sure why this is a reasonable assumption, and hence my original comments about hidden confounders in the data generation process which generated $\mathbf{X}$.  As mentioned before, one way to test this is to see if the generalisation bound close to the ideal case (Eq. 15) is achieved on a simple (possibly synthetic) dataset. Therefore, as it stands currently, there is a mismatch in claims from the theory and what the paper aims to achieve and empirically evaluate on (achieving robust generalisable representation). 

In addition, despite the revision, I feel the writeup is still a bit convoluted and confusing with regards to the entire approach. The proposed algorithm contains lot of details and they need to be explained and introduced better, rather than focusing quite significant space on arriving at IB. Small note: In the proof of Lemma 1, Equation (23) still seems to have a typo, and could be a source of confusion.
